resolved_by: Supreme Court in United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), which held that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c)(3)(A)'s elements clause
issue: Does attempted Hobbs Act robbery qualify as a crime of violence under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A)?

sides.position: Attempted Hobbs Act robbery qualifies as a crime of violence under § 924(c)(3)(A)'s elements clause (pre-Taylor view; the excerpts do not name the circuits that held this)

Attempted Hobbs Act robbery does not qualify as a crime of violence under § 924(c)(3)(A)'s elements clause, because it does not require the use, attempted use, or threatened use of force (Taylor holding, which this court applies)
cases: United States v. Bouie, No. 24-12347 (11th Cir. Dec. 22, 2025)

this_court: Attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c)(3)(A)'s elements clause, following Taylor
quote: In Taylor, the Supreme Court resolved a circuit split and held that attempted Hobbs Act robbery does not qualify as a predicate crime of violence under § 924(c)(3)(A)'s elements clause.
cite: United States v. Tyrell Bouie, No. 24-12347 (11th Cir. 2025)
